topic: China recruited AI exec to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
headline_marked: [[China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang]] for chip intelligence
headline: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang for chip intelligence
summary: China's Ministry of State Security allegedly enlisted Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to gather intelligence on American AI chips and potentially influence Nvidia's supply to China.
details: China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) reportedly recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The alleged goal was to glean information about American AI chips.

The MSS also sought to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips available to China. Alice Huang is a customer of Nvidia's and has high-level connections across the AI chip industry, including with Gigabyte executives.
The New York Times initially reported Jensen Huang as the target of a "Chinese spy plot" last week. The new information from the NYT confirms that China's MSS specifically recruited Alice Huang.

Despite having the same surname, Alice and Jensen Huang are not related, though their relationship is described as "close." Former President Trump was reportedly briefed on this relationship last year but did not take action.
Following these reports, three House committees have requested Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing. The briefing will focus on his "interactions" with Alice Huang.

The MSS also sought to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips available to China. Alice Huang is a customer of Nvidia's and has high-level connections across the AI chip industry, including with Gigabyte executives.

The New York Times initially reported Jensen Huang as the target of a "Chinese spy plot" last week. The new information from the NYT confirms that China's MSS specifically recruited Alice Huang.

Despite having the same surname, Alice and Jensen Huang are not related, though their relationship is described as "close." Former President Trump was reportedly briefed on this relationship last year but did not take action.

topic: Sodium-ion batteries near cost parity with LFP
headline_marked: [[Sodium-ion batteries approach cost parity with LFP]] by late 2026, offering 21% lower total ownership cost
headline: Sodium-ion batteries approach cost parity with LFP by late 2026, offering 21% lower total ownership cost
summary: Wood Mackenzie predicts cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by late 2026, with potential for 21% lower total cost of ownership over 20 years.
details: Sodium-ion battery technology is entering commercial production, emerging as a viable alternative to lithium-ion batteries. Supply agreements totaling over 70 GWh are already in place, according to an analysis by Wood Mackenzie.

The study identifies sodium-ion as the most promising alternative to lithium-based technologies for stationary energy storage. Leading manufacturers are expected to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by late 2026.

While current upfront costs are higher at a global average of $229/kWh compared to approximately $200/kWh for LFP, sodium-ion batteries could offer a 21% lower total cost of ownership over a 20-year project lifetime. This difference is primarily attributed to the elimination of capacity expansion cycles and lower operating costs.

Key technical advantages include raw material supply security, longer service life, and a wider operating temperature range. The latter could make them particularly suitable for applications in cold climates, where lithium-ion batteries may require additional thermal management systems.

China is leading the commercialization, with BYD planning to reach 30 GWh of sodium-ion battery manufacturing capacity. CATL aims to exceed 1 GWh in sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026, with supply agreements already in place across China, the US, and Europe.

Industrial and trade policies are playing an increasingly important role in competitiveness. China reintroduced a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries in July 2026, while exempting sodium-ion batteries until the end of 2028.

In the United States, tariffs of approximately 58% on energy storage cells imported from China, combined with production tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), are encouraging domestic sodium-ion battery manufacturing. Europe's carbon footprint declaration requirements and India's incentive programs also support the technology.

Wood Mackenzie expects the 2030–2035 period to be decisive for sodium-ion batteries to achieve full economic competitiveness. For energy storage projects currently under development, LFP remains the most commercially mature option for storage durations of two to four hours.
